content: 1. All test operators must demonstrate proficiency before participating in the study. This ensures that the testing process is conducted accurately and reliably. 2. Accurate record-keeping is essential for maintaining data quality. Transcription errors are common and should be minimized. Individual-run worksheets and consolidated worksheets must be used for comprehensive data analysis. All data entries should be double-checked for accuracy. 3. During the verification study, each product must be tested using a verification panel. Each specimen in the panel should be labeled with a unique identification number that does not reveal the expected diagnostic result. Test operators must be blinded to the expected reference results for each specimen. 4. Test operators, representative of the intended users, should follow the instructions for use (IFU), labels, and other instructional materials without assistance. If test kit controls are available, they must be used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Both lots of each product should be tested on the same verification panel. 5. For rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), the intensity of the test band should be recorded on a scale to distinguish between weak and strong test lines: 0 (non-reactive), 1+ (weakly reactive), 2+ (moderately reactive), and 3+ (strongly reactive). 6. A second reader should perform a blinded re-reading of any visually read assay after the first reader (test operator) has recorded the test result. The intensity of the test line/band should also be recorded to quantify variability due to faint test lines. If the two readers agree on the interpretation, the specimen status is recorded as is. If they disagree, a third reader should adjudicate the result. 7. If a conclusive result cannot be reached, the result should be recorded as inconclusive, and the specimen should be retested on a new test device from the same lot. These results should be included in the data analysis as misdiagnosed specimens. 8. Invalid results for visually read assays, such as RDTs, occur when the control line does not appear, regardless of the test line's appearance, or when a high background color obscures the result window. Other anomalies, such as streaking across the membrane, non-migration of the specimen, or debris on the membrane, should also be recorded. 9. For instrument-based assays, such as chemiluminescence immunoassays, invalid results or runs occur when internal and/or external test kit controls (e.g., HIV-negative or HIV-positive) fall outside the acceptance range specified in the manufacturer’s instructions. The rate of invalid test results/runs should be recorded as a proportion of the total tests/runs performed. 10. Data analysis should include calculating the rate of common false reactivity between candidate products. If no combination of products eliminates shared false-reactive results, the combination with the least common false-reactive results should be chosen. 11. The results of the verification study should remain valid for three to five years. 12. Testing algorithms must be continuously monitored for effectiveness, including any adverse events related to HIV misdiagnosis. It is recommended to run new testing algorithms in parallel with existing ones for two weeks at high-throughput testing sites or four weeks at low-throughput sites. A discrepancy rate of greater than 1% between the new and existing algorithms requires investigation of the root cause. 13. After the initial familiarization period, the testing algorithms may be rolled out more widely. Data should be collected on the rate of HIV-inconclusive status and invalid test results, with an acceptable invalid rate of no more than 5%. Any observations related to test procedures or operational characteristics that do not meet the manufacturer’s claims should be documented and reported according to WHO guidance on post-market surveillance of in vitro diagnostics (IVDs). 14. Complaints related to the products themselves should be reported to the assay manufacturer as part of post-market surveillance. 15. For individuals over two years of age, HIV diagnosis is based on the detection of antibodies to HIV and/or HIV-1 p24 antigen (serological markers) rather than the detection of the virus itself (virological markers). Where resources permit, assays detecting HIV p24 antigen only or specific types of HIV-1/HIV-2 antibodies may be used to resolve atypical diagnoses. 16. Serological assays alone are insufficient to rule in HIV infection in infants due to the potential detection of maternal antibodies transferred during pregnancy, birth, and breastfeeding. Virological testing, typically using nucleic acid testing (NAT), is recommended instead. 17. The natural history of HIV infection includes an eclipse period immediately following infection, during which no assay can detect HIV due to the minimal presence of nucleic acid and the absence of antibodies. This period typically lasts approximately 10 days. 18. The end of the eclipse period is marked by the detection of nucleic acid using NAT assays, approximately 12–14 days after infection. Shortly thereafter, immunoassays can briefly detect HIV antigen. The detection of HIV-1/2 antibodies, first immunoglobulin M (IgM) and then immunoglobulin G (IgG), signals seroconversion and the end of the diagnostic window period, which generally concludes around 21 days post-infection. 19. The duration of the diagnostic window period depends on four main factors: (1) genetic factors of the virus, (2) genetics and immunocompetence of the host, (3) assay target and detection type (antigen, IgM, or IgG antibodies), and (4) specimen type (serum, plasma, venous whole blood, capillary whole blood, or oral fluid). 20. Fourth-generation serology assays generally detect antibodies earliest, followed by third-generation and second-generation assays. First-generation serology assays using viral lysate have the longest window period. 21. In the case of HIV-1 infection, HIV-1 p24 antigen appears briefly. For HIV-2 infection, HIV-2 p26 antigen appears briefly. 22. Specimen integrity is critical for ensuring the accuracy of HIV testing. If an assay’s instructions for use do not include a specific specimen type, it indicates that the manufacturer has not validated that specimen type for use with the assay. 23. Specimen types and processing requirements vary. For example, venous whole blood should be used immediately, serum should be processed within 30 minutes of collection and stored at 2–8°C for up to five days, and plasma should be processed within six hours of collection and stored similarly. Capillary whole blood and oral fluid should be used immediately, while dried blood spot (DBS) specimens can be stored at 4°C for up to three months or at –20°C for longer periods. 24. The use of DBS specimens with specific assays must be validated by the manufacturer. If not validated, the use of DBS specimens is considered “off-label” and unauthorized for returning medical results to clients, including in the context of HIV surveillance.
